Consider a right triangle inscribed in a semi-circle of radius $\sqrt{6},$ as shown above. Find the maximum possible area ${A}_{\text{max}}$  of the triangle. Do not round the answer.

${A}_{\text{max}}=$ 
 {{field-1}}
question.worked_solution:
Let's call $l$ the length of one leg. By the Pythagorean theorem, the length of the other leg is $\sqrt{24-{l}^{2}}.$

Therefore, the area of the triangle is given by

$$
A(l)=\frac{1}{2}l\sqrt{24-{l}^{2}}\,.
$$

Since $l$ is the length of a leg of a right triangle whose hypotenuse is $2\sqrt{6}$, the permitted range of $l$ is $0<l<2\sqrt{6}.$

We want to maximize $A(l),$ so we need to compute the critical points. Taking the derivative, we get

$$
{A}^{′}(l)=\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{24-{l}^{2}}-\frac{{l}^{2}}{2\sqrt{24-{l}^{2}}}.
$$

and solving ${A}^{′}(l)=0$ gives the following critical point:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{24-{l}^{2}}-\frac{{l}^{2}}{2\sqrt{24-{l}^{2}}} & =0 \\ 24-{l}^{2}-{l}^{2} & =0 \\ 2{l}^{2} & =24 \\ {l}^{2} & =12 \\ l & =2\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

All that's left now is to confirm that $l=2\sqrt{3}$ does indeed give a maximum value of $A(l).$ To do this, we use the first derivative test. We write up a table of values:

| Interval | $(0,2\sqrt{3})$ | $2\sqrt{3}$ | $(2\sqrt{3},2\sqrt{6})$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $1$ | $$ | $4$ |
| ${A}^{′}$ | $+$ | $0$ | $-$ |
| $A$ | $↗$ | $\text{max}$ | $↘$ |

So, $l=2\sqrt{3}$ does indeed give a maximum, and the area of the resulting triangle will be the largest possible.

Finally, the maximum possible area ${A}_{\text{max}}$  is

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{\text{max}}=A(2\sqrt{3}) & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\sqrt{3}\cdot \sqrt{24-(2\sqrt{3})^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\sqrt{3}\cdot \sqrt{24-12} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\sqrt{3}\cdot \sqrt{12} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\sqrt{3}\cdot 2\sqrt{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 12 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$
